799.title: Savitri and Satyavan
799.hook: Savitri walks behind Yama, talking, and Death keeps stopping to offer her gifts
799.carry: ask a favor on someone else's behalf
799.howItsDone: In the epic, each gift Yama offers Savitri on the road follows a speech of hers about dharma and the good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri and Satyavan: his head in her lap, Yama with his noose, and Savitri getting up to follow. Your line was sit with someone tired, without fixing. Did you sit with someone tired? Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

Yama hears footsteps behind him. He is heading south with Satyavan's life bound in his noose, and someone is following. He turns. Go back, Savitri, he tells her. Go and perform his last rites. You have come as far as anyone can come. She doesn't argue about the distance. She talks about something else entirely. And Death stops to listen. Behind them, in the clearing, Satyavan's body lies still under the trees.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS BEHIND DEATH.` → `GO BACK, SAVITRI.` → `DEATH STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Savitri's first answer is simple. Where my husband is taken, I go too. That is the old way. And then she says something about friendship. The wise say, she tells him, that walking seven steps together makes people friends. We have walked more than that, you and I. So, as a friend, hear me. Then she speaks about dharma, the right way, and about the good, the people who keep it. Yama is pleased. Ask for a gift, he says. Anything except his life. Savitri doesn't ask for herself. Her father-in-law is blind and living in the forest. Let him see, she says. Granted. Now go back, Yama says, you're worn out. How could I be tired, she answers, when I'm walking beside my husband? And she keeps talking: about how good it is to be near the good, even for a moment. Yama is pleased again. Another gift, anything but his life. Give my father-in-law back his kingdom, she says. Granted. She speaks again, about how the good are kind even to those who wrong them. A third gift. Her own father has no sons, so she asks for sons for him. Granted. Notice the pattern. Every gift goes to someone else. And every time, what moves Yama isn't her grief. It's what she says about goodness, said to Death himself, on the road. She hasn't asked for Satyavan once. Not yet.
screen: `WHERE HE GOES, I GO.` · `SEVEN STEPS MAKE A FRIEND.` · `SIGHT, THEN A KINGDOM, THEN SONS.` · then, large: `EVERY GIFT FOR SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: If you have room, stand and take seven slow steps, then sit down again. If not, take seven slow breaths where you are. Bring to mind someone you've walked beside for a long time: a friend, a partner, a sibling. Let one good thing about them come forward. Then, without needing to say it out loud, think of one thing you'd ask for on their behalf, not your own. Breathe in, and hold them in mind. Breathe out, and let the wish go with them. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sat, the good, the true. Today, Savitri walks behind Death, talking about the good, and asking every gift for someone else.
Your line: ask a favor on someone else's behalf. Today, if someone offers you a favor, ask for it on behalf of someone else. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: Savitri and Satyavan
800.hook: the last gift, Satyavan's life given back, and a long walk home through the dark
800.howItsDone: Markandeya ends the story by turning back to Yudhishthira's question about Draupadi; outside the epic, some married women honor Savitri on Vat Savitri with a fast and threads tied around a banyan tree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri and Satyavan: three gifts from Death, sight, a kingdom and sons, and every one for someone else. Your line was ask a favor on someone else's behalf. Did you ask a favor for someone else? Day eight hundred.
screen: `SAVITRI AND SATYAVAN.` · `THREE GIFTS, ALL GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ask once more, says Death. Savitri is still on the road behind Yama, still talking. And this time she asks for something for herself. Let me have sons, she says, sons of my own, born of Satyavan. Yama grants it. So be it. Then she keeps walking. She keeps speaking about the good. And now a gift has been given that can only come true one way. And the noose in Yama's hand is still closed.
screen: `ASK ONCE MORE.` → `SONS, BORN OF SATYAVAN.` → `SO BE IT.`

segments.voice: It's easy to hear this as a clever trap: Death says yes too fast and gets caught. In the epic it reads more like a conversation won. Savitri speaks again about the good, how they keep to the truth and hold the world up, and Yama is pleased once more. Ask for something beyond compare, he says. And Savitri asks plainly. The gift you gave me can't happen without my husband. Without him I don't want happiness, or heaven, or even my own life. Let Satyavan live. And Yama loosens the noose. He gives Satyavan back, blesses them both with a long life together, and goes on his way. Savitri walks back to the clearing, sits down, and takes her husband's head into her lap again. Satyavan opens his eyes like a man waking from a long sleep. Why didn't you wake me, he asks. Where's the dark one who was dragging me away? It's night now. The forest is full of sounds. He's frightened for his parents, who will be out of their minds with worry. So Savitri ties up her hair, helps him to his feet, picks up his axe, and they walk home in the dark, his arm over her shoulder. At the hermitage, his father has his sight back, and he and his wife have been searching, and the hermits have been telling them Satyavan must be alive. Savitri tells them everything. And this is why the sage Markandeya told the story in the first place. Yudhishthira had asked him whether any woman had been as devoted as Draupadi. Like Savitri, Markandeya says, Draupadi will save you all.
screen: `A CONVERSATION WON, NOT A TRAP.` · `WITHOUT HIM I DON'T WANT HEAVEN.` · `WAKING, AND THE WALK HOME.` · then, large: `DRAUPADI WILL SAVE YOU ALL.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind someone who is still here with you: someone you can call, or sit beside, or walk home with. Let their face come clear. Breathe in, and notice that they're here. Breathe out, and let gladness about that fill the breath, quietly, without needing a reason. If someone you've lost comes to mind instead, let them come, and hold them kindly too. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Savitri and Satyavan. A wife who talked with Death until he gave her husband back, and a walk home through the dark. Today's words.
Your line: Savitri and Satyavan. Today, tell one person who's still here that you're glad they are. Day eight hundred.

801.title: the Yaksha's questions
801.hook: a deer runs off with a brahmin's fire-sticks, the brothers chase it into thirst, and a voice at a lake says: answer first
801.howItsDone: The Yaksha's questions are a dialogue on dharma set in the Pandavas' forest years, and the episode opens with the brothers' chase to recover a brahmin's fire-sticks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri and Satyavan came home through the dark, and Markandeya told Yudhishthira that Draupadi would save them all. Your line was Savitri and Satyavan. Who did you tell you were glad they're here? Day eight hundred one.

A pair of fire-sticks, swinging from a deer's antlers. A brahmin comes running to the Pandavas in their forest exile. He had left his arani, the two pieces of wood he rubs together to kindle his sacred fire, hanging on a tree. A deer came by, rubbed against the tree, and the sticks caught in its antlers. Now it's bounding away with them. Without them, he can't keep his fire. The five brothers take up their bows and go after it, deeper into the trees than any of them meant to go.
screen: `FIRE-STICKS ON A DEER'S ANTLERS.` → `A BRAHMIN'S FIRE AT STAKE.` → `FIVE BROTHERS GIVE CHASE.`

segments.voice: The deer stays just out of reach. The brothers shoot and miss, chase and fall behind, and then it's simply gone. They sink down under a tree, exhausted and parched. And in that low moment the talk turns sour. Nakula asks why trouble keeps finding a family that has tried to live rightly. One by one the brothers remember the dice hall and what they failed to do there. Yudhishthira says only that misfortune has no limits, and no one can say where it comes from. Then he turns practical. Nakula, he says, climb that tree and look for water. Nakula climbs and sees green plants and cranes, the signs of water not far off. He goes alone, to bring some back. He finds a lake, clear and still. He is about to drink when a voice speaks from nowhere. Don't be rash, child. This lake is mine. Answer my questions first, then drink and take as much as you like. Nakula is burning with thirst. He doesn't stop. He kneels, drinks, and falls down dead on the bank. So the episode begins, not with a riddle, but with a duty: a brother running after someone else's fire. And it reaches its crisis with a plain temptation, water to a thirsty man, and one voice asking him to pause first. The questions haven't been asked yet. Today, only the door: the lake, the voice, and a brother who didn't wait to hear them.
screen: `A CHASE THAT COMES TO NOTHING.` · `NAKULA CLIMBS AND SEES CRANES.` · `THIS LAKE IS MINE. ANSWER FIRST.` · then, large: `HE DRINKS, AND FALLS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath come and go. If there's a glass of water near you, set it where you can see it. If not, picture one. Let it wait there, the way the lake waited in front of Nakula. Ask yourself one plain question: what do I actually need right now? Don't hurry the answer. Breathe in, and ask. Breathe out, and listen. When the bell rings, drink slowly, if you like. If you pray, you can offer that pause in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Yaksha's questions. A voice at a lake that asks before it lets anyone drink, and a brother too thirsty to listen. Today's words.
Your line: the Yaksha's questions. Today, before your first drink of water, stop and ask yourself one honest question. Day eight hundred one.

802.title: the Yaksha's questions
802.hook: one by one the brothers go to the lake, each with his own strength, and each ignores the voice
802.howItsDone: In the epic, the four brothers fall one by one before Yudhishthira arrives, each warned by the same voice in the same words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yaksha's questions began with a stolen pair of fire-sticks, and Nakula drank before he listened. Your line was the Yaksha's questions. Did you stop and ask yourself a question before that first drink of water? Day eight hundred two.

Nakula doesn't come back. Under the tree, his brothers wait, and wait, and Yudhishthira sends the next one. Sahadeva, go and find your brother, and bring water. So Sahadeva follows the cranes to the lake. And there is Nakula, lying on the bank. Sahadeva is grieving, and he is burning with thirst, and the voice speaks again, the same words. This lake is mine. Answer first. Back under the tree, three brothers are still waiting for water.
screen: `NAKULA DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `SAHADEVA GOES NEXT.` → `THE SAME VOICE, THE SAME WORDS.`

segments.voice: Sahadeva drinks, and falls beside his brother. Now Yudhishthira sends Arjuna, the great archer. Arjuna reaches the lake with his bow ready, and sees both twins dead. He looks around for an enemy and sees no one. When the voice speaks, Arjuna does what a warrior does. He shoots at it. He sends arrows toward the sound, aiming by ear alone. The voice answers, unhurt: your arrows can't touch me. Answer my questions, and then drink. Arjuna drinks, and falls. Then Bhima comes, the strong one. He sees three brothers on the ground and decides this must be the work of some spirit, and that he'll fight whoever it is. But first, water. The voice warns him too. He doesn't listen. He drinks, and falls. Notice what each one brings. Nakula brings his thirst. Sahadeva brings his grief. Arjuna brings an archer's perfect aim. Bhima brings his strength, and a plan to fight. And not one of them brings what the voice asked for: a moment to listen, and an answer. The lake doesn't want to be conquered. It wants to be answered. Each brother meets it with his own best gift, and for this lake it's the wrong gift. That's the story's warning. Four heroes of the Mahabharata lie on a lakeshore because they wouldn't stop to hear a question. One brother is left.
screen: `SAHADEVA DRINKS, AND FALLS.` · `ARJUNA SHOOTS AT THE VOICE.` · `BHIMA PLANS TO FIGHT, BUT DRINKS.` · then, large: `IT WANTS TO BE ANSWERED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and close your eyes if you like. Let the sounds around you arrive: traffic, a fan, a voice in another room, your own breath. Notice how quickly the mind wants to aim at each one, name it, judge it, do something about it. Don't. Just let each sound come, and go, unanswered and unshot. Breathe in, and hear. Breathe out, and let the sound pass. If you pray, you can rest in that listening as a kind of prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Yaksha's questions. Four brothers bring thirst, grief, aim and strength, and none of them stops to listen. Today's words.
Your line: the Yaksha's questions. Today, when something pushes back at you, ask what it actually wants before you push harder. Day eight hundred two.

803.title: the Yaksha's questions
803.hook: Yudhishthira reaches the lake, reads the scene, and agrees to answer; the questions begin
803.howItsDone: In the epic, the yaksha's questions often sound like riddles, and Yudhishthira's answers keep pointing back to family, mind and conduct.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yaksha's questions went unanswered four times: thirst, grief, aim and strength, and four brothers on the shore. Your line was the Yaksha's questions. Did you ask what something wanted before pushing? Day eight hundred three.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `FOUR BROTHERS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: The last brother comes alone. Yudhishthira has waited under the tree as long as he can, and now he follows the cranes himself. He finds the lake, and all four of his brothers lying beside it. He weeps over each of them by name, and remembers what each one was to him. And then, through his grief, he does something none of them did. He looks. Before he touches the water, he reads the shore.
screen: `THE LAST BROTHER COMES ALONE.` → `HE WEEPS OVER EACH ONE.` → `THEN HE LOOKS.`

segments.voice: What Yudhishthira sees doesn't add up. There are no wounds on his brothers. There are no footprints of an enemy. Their faces haven't changed color, so he doesn't think it's poison. Whatever did this, he reasons, is something greater than an ordinary foe. He steps down into the water, and the voice comes. I am a crane, it says. I killed your brothers. Answer my questions, or you'll be the fifth. Yudhishthira doesn't believe it. No bird could do this, he says. Who are you? And then he sees it: a yaksha, a huge spirit, towering over the lake, speaking from up in a tree. Yudhishthira doesn't shoot, or fight, or drink. He says something quiet instead. I don't want what's yours. Ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able. And so the questions begin. Some of them sound like riddles. What is heavier than the earth? Yudhishthira answers: a mother. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than blades of grass? Our thoughts. Look at what those four answers do. The yaksha asks about the size of the world, and Yudhishthira answers with a family, and a mind. Weight becomes a mother's claim on us. Height becomes a father's. Speed and number turn inward, to what happens behind the eyes. The questions point outward, and the answers come home. Watch for that in the answers still to come.
screen: `NO WOUNDS, NO FOOTPRINTS.` · `I AM A CRANE. WHO ARE YOU?` · `I'LL ANSWER AS WELL AS I'M ABLE.` · then, large: `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow down. Now watch your thoughts arrive, the way you'd watch blades of grass in a field: one, then another, then too many to follow. Don't count them. Don't pick any up. Just notice how many there are, and how fast the mind runs after them, faster than the wind, as Yudhishthira says. Breathe in, and see a thought. Breathe out, and let it go back into the field. If you pray, you can let the thoughts pass through your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Yaksha's questions. The brother who stops to look, offers to answer, and turns every question about the world back home. Today's words.
Your line: the Yaksha's questions. Today, before you react to something that looks wrong, look closely once more. Day eight hundred three.

804.title: the Yaksha's questions
804.hook: the questions turn from riddles to friends: who stands by the traveler, the householder, the sick and the dying
804.howItsDone: The middle of the Yaksha's questions mixes riddles about fish and rivers with plain guidance: who our friends are in each season, and what is worth giving up.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yaksha's questions began: heavier than the earth, a mother; faster than the wind, the mind. Your line was the Yaksha's questions. Did you look twice before reacting? Day eight hundred four.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: What sleeps with its eyes open? The yaksha keeps going, and some of the questions are pure fun. Yudhishthira answers: a fish. What doesn't move once it's born? An egg. What has no heart? A stone. What grows by its own force? A river. Four brothers lie dead on the shore, and the conversation sounds almost like a game by a campfire. But listen to where it goes next. The yaksha is still asking, and Yudhishthira is still answering, one plain word at a time.
screen: `WHAT SLEEPS WITH ITS EYES OPEN?` → `A FISH, AN EGG, A STONE, A RIVER.` → `THEN, WHO STANDS BY US?`

segments.voice: Who is the friend of a traveler far from home? the yaksha asks. Yudhishthira answers: a companion on the road. Who is the friend of someone who keeps a home? The wife. Who is the friend of someone who is sick? The physician. And who is the friend of someone about to die? Charity, the gifts they've given. Four friends for four seasons of a life. It's an unglamorous list. No heroes, no gods, no armies. Just a person beside you on the road, the one you share a house with, the healer at the bedside, and at the very end, what you gave away. Remember who is answering. Yudhishthira is in exile himself, far from home, a long way from any kingdom. His companions on the road are lying dead behind him. The answer about the traveler isn't abstract for him. Then the yaksha asks about letting go. What, if you give it up, makes you agreeable? Pride, Yudhishthira says. What, given up, leaves no regret? Anger. What makes you rich, once you let it go? Desire. And what makes you happy, once it's gone? Greed. Notice how practical these are. The yaksha isn't asking about heaven yet. He's asking how to be good company, and how not to be miserable. The epic sets these answers in the mouth of a man whose brothers' lives depend on getting them right, and they come out plain and small, the kind of thing you could live by on an ordinary day.
screen: `A COMPANION FOR THE TRAVELER.` · `A HEALER FOR THE SICK.` · `CHARITY FOR THE DYING.` · then, large: `GIVE UP PRIDE, ANGER, DESIRE, GREED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind, one at a time, the friends of your own seasons. Someone who was a companion when you were far from home. Someone who shares, or shared, your home. Someone who looked after you when you were sick. Let each face come and stay for a few breaths. Breathe in, and remember them. Breathe out, and thank them silently. If you pray, you can hold each one in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Yaksha's questions. A fish that sleeps with open eyes, four friends for four seasons, and four things worth letting go. Today's words.
Your line: the Yaksha's questions. Today, send a word of thanks to one person who was your companion when you were far from home. Day eight hundred four.

805.title: the Yaksha's questions
805.hook: four big questions: who is happy, what is the wonder, what is the path, and what is the news
805.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's answer about what is wonderful, that people see others die every day and still live as if they never will, is the line some readers carry away from the whole episode.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yaksha's questions turned to friends: a companion for the traveler, a healer for the sick, charity for the dying. Your line was the Yaksha's questions. Who did you thank? Day eight hundred five.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `A FRIEND FOR EVERY SEASON.`

segments.voice: Four more questions, and they're the big ones. The yaksha has asked about the sun and the earth, about friends and anger and greed. Now he asks Yudhishthira four questions in a row. Who is happy? What is wonderful? What is the path? And what is the news? Four brothers are still lying on the shore. The answers have to be true, not clever, and Yudhishthira gives each one in a sentence or two.
screen: `WHO IS HAPPY?` → `WHAT IS WONDERFUL?` → `WHAT IS THE PATH? WHAT IS THE NEWS?`

segments.voice: Who is happy? Yudhishthira's answer is wonderfully small. The person who cooks simple greens in their own home, late in the day, who owes nothing to anyone, and who doesn't have to live away from home. Hear that from a prince in exile: happiness is a modest supper under your own roof, with no debts. What is the path? Here he's honest about how hard it is. Argument doesn't settle it. The scriptures say different things. There isn't one sage whose view everyone accepts. The truth of dharma, he says, is hidden as if in a cave. So the path is the one the great have walked. What is the news? He answers with a picture. The world is a great cooking pot. Time is the cook, with the sun for fire and days and nights for fuel, stirring every creature with the months and seasons for a ladle. And then: what is wonderful? Every day, living beings go to the house of Death, and those who are left live as if they never will. What could be more wonderful than that? Not a complaint. A wonder. He's describing the ones still here, cheerfully making plans while the pot simmers. A look back over the week: it began with Savitri on the road, talking with Death until he gave her husband back. It ends here, with a brother talking with a stranger at a lake, his brothers' lives hanging on his answers. Two conversations, and in both, the one who listens and speaks truly is the one who saves the others.
screen: `HAPPY: GREENS AT HOME, AND NO DEBTS.` · `THE PATH: THE ONE THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.` · `THE NEWS: TIME COOKS EVERY CREATURE.` · then, large: `THE WONDER: WE LIVE AS IF WE WON'T DIE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your breathing slow. Notice that this breath is one you'll never take again. Not sadly. Just notice it, the way Yudhishthira notices the wonder. Breathe in, and feel this one. Breathe out, and let it go. Then the next, also new. Let a little gladness come with each one, for the plain fact of being here now, in your own home or wherever you are. If you pray, you can give thanks in your prayer for this breath. The bell holds the time.
The Yaksha's questions. Supper at home with no debts, a path the great have walked, time stirring the pot, and the wonder that we live as if we never die. Today's words.
Your line: the Yaksha's questions. Tonight, eat one simple meal slowly, and count it as the happiness Yudhishthira names. Day eight hundred five.

myth: Yudhishthira said the path is found by argument
he said argument doesn't settle it and the scriptures differ, so follow the path the great have walked.
in his answer, happiness is a simple meal at home with no debts
and not having to live away from home.
the wonder, he said, is the sun rising each day
it's that people see others die every day and still live as if they never will.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. the yaksha asks: what is the path? you know the scriptures differ and arguments go in circles. what do you answer?
options: whatever the oldest scripture says.
the one the great have walked.
whatever reason proves best.
fork.reveal: the truth of dharma is hidden as if in a cave, he says, so the path is the one the great have walked.

trapdoor: what you thought: a single line about death.
what it means: four plain answers about happiness, the path, time and wonder, given with four brothers' lives at stake.
what a scholar hears: on the path, Yudhishthira concedes that argument is unsettled, the scriptures differ, and no single sage's view is accepted by all.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: the last four questions (who is happy, what is wonderful, what is the path, what is the news)
